Conclusion

  • An on-premises Kubernetes cluster must include a shared storage solution to support stateful workloads. SAN, NAS, or software-defined storage are more essential than ever in these infrastructures. Beyond enabling data mobility across cluster nodes, these solutions can also provide advanced data services that cloud-hosted options may not offer to Kubernetes—such as volume-based replication, high IOPS, high-bandwidth volumes, and more.

Container Storage Interface & Dell Container Storage Modules

  • With the release of Kubernetes 1.13, the Container Storage Interface (CSI) promoted to GA status.

    The CSI specification standardizes persistent storage management (block or file) within container orchestrators. One key advantage of CSI over “in-tree” drivers is that CSI Driver development is decoupled from Kubernetes releases, offering greater flexibility and agility in driver evolution.

    The CSI documentation covers many aspects of storage management, including volume provisioning and decommissioning, snapshot management, volume health metrics, filesystem permissions, and more.

    However, many advanced data services offered by PowerMax are not yet covered by the CSI specification. To expose these additional features, Dell developed the Container Storage Modules (CSM).

    CSM components are typically deployed as additional sidecar containers alongside the CSI PowerMax driver, or as separate containers within the same cluster.

    Dell Container Storage Modules form an evolving ecosystem. The official documentation is available at : https://dell.github.io/csm-docs/docs/

    Dell is committed to releasing updated versions of the CSI Driver approximately every 90 days. Both CSI and CSM modules are fully open source and supported by Dell through official support (https://www.dell.com/support).

CSI for PowerMax

  • At the time of the publication of that paper, the CSI Driver for PowerMax is compatible with CSI v1.6 and offers the capabilities of :

    • Volume lifecycle (Create, Delete, Clone, Expand size)
    • Snapshot lifecycle (Create, Restore in PVC, Delete)
    • Provision Ephemeral volumes & Raw block device
    • Storage Topology (i.e. schedule workload only on nodes which as the connectivity to the array)
    • Multiple Availability Zones (i.e. one StorageClass for connecting to PowerMax arrays in different topology zones)
    • Volume Health Monitoring & Volume Limits tracking

    You can refer to the support matrix for the most up-to-date information on CSI compatibility & features.

CSM for Authorization

  • CSM for Authorization is the most effective way to enable fine-grained quotas for Kubernetes clusters consuming PowerMax storage.

    CSM for Authorization enables storage backend multi-tenancy by letting storage and Kubernetes administrators the ability to:

    • Declare tenants to restrict the usage of storage (usually one per Kubernetes cluster)
    • Apply RBAC policies to resources created by the tenant
    • Authenticate tenants with a JSON Web Token

    To support these use-cases we need to deploy a proxy between the tenants (CSI drivers) and the storage system.

    Once a policy is configured or modified by the storage administrator, it applies immediately.

    To enforce a secure and distributed responsibility model, different stakeholders are assigned specific roles:

    • Storage Administrators: Responsible for creating, deleting, and managing roles/groups to which storage policies are applied.
    • Kubernetes Administrators and Users: Can generate authentication tokens. These tokens allow Kubernetes administrators to access storage with the appropriate access policies automatically enforced.
    • Privileged Access Management (PAM) Administrators: Define how storage credentials are obtained.
    • DevOps Administrators: Implement the workflow for managing the lifecycle of the entire process. A GitOps agent is recommended to distribute the various configuration elements.

    The usual sequence when using CSM for Authorization is to:

    1. Storage Endpoint Declaration
      The Storage Administrator declares the storage endpoints that Kubernetes users should be allowed to access. They collaborate with the Privileged Access Management (PAM) Administrator to define how to obtain the credentials. This results in:
      1. A csm-authorization.storage.dell.com/v1 Storage resource
      2. A Secret containing the credentials, either as a native Kubernetes resource or retrieved via the CSI Secret Provider from a PAM or Secrets Management system.
    2. Cluster and Quota Agreement
      The Storage Administrator and Kubernetes Administrator agree on the list of Kubernetes clusters and their associated quotas. This results in:
      1. A csm-authorization.storage.dell.com/v1 CSMRole with the Quota in GiB
      2. Multiple csm-authorization.storage.dell.com/v1 Tenants  resources, each linked to a CSMRole and a volume prefix to identify them
      3. Multiple Secret containing JWTs, to be loaded on each cluster for CSI drivers to authenticate against the Authorization proxy.
    3. Lifecycle Implementation
      The DevOps Administrator and Kubernetes Administrator implement the lifecycle management of the various objects (e.g., CSI driver configuration, quota updates). Recommended outcomes include:
      1. A Git repository with merge rules (e.g., only the Storage Administrator can modify quotas, subject to approval by the Kubernetes cluster owner).
      2. A GitOps agent such as ArgoCD or FluxCD to deploy the CSI driver and apply resource changes.

    Note: A single token can be shared by multiple Kubernetes clusters resulting in sharing the same Quota and Objects

CSM for PowerMax

  • At the time of the publication of that paper, the CSM modules for PowerMax are:

    • Replication to implement and expose SRDF capabilities to the Kubernetes users
    • Authorization to offer RBAC, credential shielding and fine-grained quotas for CSI provisioned LUN
    • Observability to expose Storage Pool & Volume performance metrics, Array & Storage Pool capacity
    • Resiliency to reschedule Stateful Pod upon Node Ungraceful Shutdown

    The CSM for Authorization feature usage is detailed in the related chapters of this document.

CSM for replication

  • CSM Replication goal is to allow the implementation of a disaster recovery plan using volume level replication with SRDF.

    Kubernetes and CSI primitives have no awareness of PersistentVolume replication. The Dell Container Storage Module Replication aims to expose all the management operations of the volume replication in Kubernetes with the help of Custom Resource Definitions.

    For the Kubernetes user, the CSM for Replication enables the provisioning of SRDF replicated volumes with a normal PVC directive. The YAML definition for the Persistent Volume Claim is just like a non-replicated volume. The only requirement is to refer to the StorageClass for the correct mode of replication. 

    While the Kubernetes administrator will use CRD extensions to launch replication operations like failover, re-protect, failback, etc.

    The CSM replication module for PowerMax will take care of the management and creation of the PV & PVC objects of the volume and replicas in the different clusters, not the workload related resources like StatefulSet, ConfigMap, Secret, and anything else that is needed by the containerized application to be running.

    The different Kubernetes cluster topologies are extensively discussed in the official documentation. But in nutshell the supported Kubernetes architectures are:

    With current CSM replication version (v1.2 at the time of the release of this white paper), several restrictions apply.

    First, PowerMax active-active metro SRDF is not possible with two independent clusters.

    With current CSM replication version (v1.2 at the time of the release of this white paper), several restrictions apply. 

    • PowerMax active-active metro SRDF is not possible with two independent clusters. 
    • SRDF groups must be preconfigured by the storage administrator for use with CSM replication modules and defined in the Storage Class (cf. Figure 2 PowerMax StorageClass with Optional values).

    Depending on the type of replication you use you have to manage the SRDF groups differently : 

    • For SRDF Synchronous mode, one SRDF group can have RDF pairing from many namespaces 
    • For SRDF Metro and Asynchronous mode, one SRDF group can only have RDF pairing from one namespace.  Failover granularity is at the namespace. 
    • Consequently, for SRDF Metro & Asynchronous modes the Kubernetes administrator have to create one StorageClass per namespace which needs to use replication. 

    For more details on the architecture, support matrix and can refer to the architecture chapter of the CSM replication documentation.

Design and architecture

  • CSI Drivers are applications that implement gRPC services as described in the CSI specification.

    They are the glue between the Kubernetes claim for storage and the storage backend.

    The CSI Driver for PowerMax is made of two components:

    • the controller which communicates to the Unisphere API to manage the storage (create/delete LUN, masking views, snapshots, etc.)
    • the node which will format and mount the LUN

    The controller can run in a high availability mode with multiple instances executed in parallel. They run in an active-passive mode and the coordination to select the active Pod uses a Lease. To identify the active controller (which can useful if you need to check logs) you can run kubectl get leases -n powermax and the holder is the active one.

Disaster recovery strategy

  • The advent of Kubernetes clustering & scheduling technologies allowed us to easily deploy stateless applications and make them highly available. Still for the stateful application, it is important to define a disaster recovery plan.

    There is a fairly wide range of possible architecture and patterns to implement a disaster recovery that is compatible with user business constraints (time to recover, capabilities of the application, distance between sites, etc.).

    In the following chapter we will explore different options that are possible with Dell CSI/CSM components.

Driver sidecars

  • Deployment of CSI/CSM is done through Sidecars containers. Some of these containers are mandatory (dark blue) by the CSI specification, others are optional and enabled by default (turquoise), or optional and disabled by default (light blue). The latter enable certain features that can be standard CSI or Dell extensions for Container Storage Modules.

    Each sidecar as a specific task to either boilerplate generic functions or execute actions; in the case of the controller, we have:

    • The controller driver which sends API calls to Unisphere.
    • The provisioner which watches the Kubernetes API server for PersistentVolumeClaim objects. If a claim appears the registrar will create the volume, if a claim disappears the registrar will remove the volume.
    • The attacher which watches the Kubernetes API server for VolumeAttachment objects and then Publish/Unpublish the volumes.
    • The resizer which watches for the volume expansion requests.
    • The snapshotter which deals with the volume snapshot related requests (create, restore in new PVC and delete)
    • The volume health to expose metrics (volume size & used, inodes used, etc.) to kube-state API.
    • The Dell Replication which watches for Dell Replication Controller requests and take care of provision replicated LUN or trigger failover/failback action.
    • The Dell Reverse Proxy is a reverse proxy specific to the CSI Driver for PowerMax. It helps to load-balance API requests between multiple Unisphere endpoints and threshold the requests to the endpoints.
    • The Dell Authorization Proxy communicates with the CSM for Authorization.

Geo-distributed Kubernetes architectures

  • The two most popular approaches to run Kubernetes workloads on different sites are to have :

    • Two or more clusters between sites running independently
    • One stretched cluster with nodes running across sites

    Note: certain Kubernetes distributions like OpenShift impose a low latency between sites to allow stretched clusters.
    The same goes with SRDF where latency is a constraint more or less relaxed depending on the type.

Host configuration

  • The CSI driver relies on the host capabilities and configuration to access the storage protocol.

    Therefore, the driver comes with pre-requisites and limitations to access the storage backend.

    Multipathing

    Multipathing is a key part of the host configuration ; the CSI Driver for PowerMax relies on Device Mapper Multipathing for iSCSI & FC and on Native multipathing for NVMe.

    iSCSI & CHAP

    If you use iSCSI with Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP), it is important to note that the configuration of the credentials is not done in the iscsid.conf but within a configuration of the driver.

    For more details on PowerMax iSCSI configuration you can refer to:   https://www.delltechnologies.com/asset/en-us/products/storage/industry-market/h14531-dell-emc-powermax-iscsi-implementation.pdf.

    Zoning Best Practices for Write Intensive Workloads

    The number of directors allocated to each host should reflect the specific demands of the workload. For write-intensive environments, such as OpenShift Virtualization, each node should be zoned to a port on every available director on the PowerMax to maximize throughput and ensure consistent performance.

    The reason is that the director receiving a write I/O is responsible for destaging it to disk. Limiting nodes to a subset of directors can cause performance bottlenecks, increasing CPU utilization and degrading array response times.

    Mapping to all directors distributes writes, allowing PowerMax’s multipathing software to balance I/O automatically and maintain even utilization across directors.

    If you experience high CPU usage on directors or on Unisphere, it is recommended to run audit with tools like Live Optics, Unisphere dashboards under support >Management server resources, additionally Unisphere REST API logging can be enabled from the support section in Unisphere for analysis by Dell support staff.

    Fiber Channel access for Virtual Machines running in VMware ESXi

    Since version v2.5.0, the CSI Driver for PowerMax allows creating LUNs that are accessible in Fiber Channel by VMware ESXi Virtual Machines using Raw Device Mapping functionality.

    That feature is named “Auto RDM over FC” in CSI/CSM documentation.

    The concept is that the CSI driver will connect to both Unisphere and vSphere API to create the respective objects.

    Once deployed with “Auto-RDM” the driver can only function in that mode, this is not possible to combine iSCSI and FC access within the same driver installation.

    The same limitation as for RDM usage applies. You can learn more about it from VMware website.

    Note: The driver needs a single initiator group to be deployed (not host group, not cascaded initiator group). Also, vMotion is not supported at this stage.

Overview

  • As applications are increasingly deployed as containers, infrastructure teams are tasked with effectively managing these workloads and supporting modern DevOps workflows. The introduction of Container Storage Interface (CSI) standard brought much-needed consistency, enabling storage vendors to develop plugins for their platforms. This allows infrastructure and DevOps teams to quickly provision and manage storage for containerized applications.

    In addition to CSI’s standard capabilities, Dell offers a set of open-source modules called Dell Container Storage Modules (CSM), which improve data services and the storage management experience in Kubernetes.  Additional CSM functionality enhances the offering beyond the base CSI standard.

    In this context, the role of storage administrators as key enablers of operational agility is more relevant than ever. This white paper outlines common storage workflows in Kubernetes environments using the Dell PowerMax storage platform. It also provides an overview of the concepts, architecture, and best practices for implementing and using the CSI Driver for the PowerMax and CSM as persistent storage within a Kubernetes cluster.

Home > Workload Solutions > Kubernetes > Canonical Kubernetes > Guides > PowerMax for Kubernetes: Architecture, CSI Integration, and Best Practices > Persistent Volume

Persistent Volume

  • A PersistentVolume (PV) is a logical volume that is provisioned to containerized applications that require persistent storage. A PV usually corresponds to a single volume on the physical storage platform.

    A PersistentVolume can be statically provisioned by the storage administrator or dynamically provisioned by the application owner with a PersistentVolumeClaim.

    It is the role of the CSI Driver for PowerMax, to create, format and bind the volume to the Kubernetes worker node and attached container.

    NAME             CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM                        STORAGECLASS   REASON   AGE

    k8s-3401e3645a   8Gi        RWO            Delete           Bound    default/pgdata-pgset-2       powermax                36d

    k8s-792f388c66   8Gi        RWO            Delete           Bound    test/pvol0                   powermax                21d

    k8s-792fe33166   16Gi       RWO            Delete           Bound    test/pvol1                   powermax-xfs            21d

    k8s-c71377055a   8Gi        RWO            Delete           Bound    default/pgdata-pgset-0       powermax                36d

    k8s-c9c63c835a   8Gi        RWO            Delete           Bound    default/pgdata-pgset-1       powermax                36d

    Figure 3.   Listing Persistent Volumes with kubectl get pv command

    Note: ReadWriteMany as you can see the PV name as a prefix (k8s in this example)
    It is a good practice to use that prefix to identify easily or uniquely the cluster that provision the volume.
    It makes the reconstruction easier in case of a disaster on the Kubernetes cluster.

Home > Workload Solutions > Kubernetes > Canonical Kubernetes > Guides > PowerMax for Kubernetes: Architecture, CSI Integration, and Best Practices > Persistent Volume Claim

Persistent Volume Claim

  • A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a request to provision storage. A PersistentVolume with the right size and StorageClass is provisioned to fulfil the request.

    Figure 4 shows an example of a PVC definition output from kubectl get pvc {{pvc_name}} 

    kubectl get pvc pgdata-pgset-0 -o yaml

    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim

    apiVersion: v1

    metadata:

      name: pgdata-pgset-0

    spec:

      storageClassName: powermax

      accessModes:

        - ReadWriteOnce

    volumeMode: Filesystem 

    resources:

        requests:

          storage: 10Gi

    Figure 4.   Example PVC definition output from kubectl get pvc command

    The key attributes for a PVC that can be modified are:

    • accessModes : defines how the volume will be read or written per Pod
    • volumeMode : has two values, Filesystem (default) or Block. Block allows to provision raw block device; it is then up to the workload to format that volume.
    • resources.requests.storage : sets the capacity claimed by the PVC

    Note: ReadWriteMany access mode cannot be used with volumeMode: Filesystem  because neither ext4 nor xfs are a clustered file system. Every over mode including ReadWriteOncePod and ReadWriteMany with volumeMode: Block work with the CSI driver for PowerMax.

    To obtain the mapped PV to a PVC you can run kubectl get pvc pgdata-pgset-0

    NAME             STATUS    VOLUME            CAPACITY     ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS                 AGE

    pgdata-pgset-0   Bound     pmax-f4a51a53b0   10487040Ki   RWO            powermax                     14s

    Note: as you can see from this example the provisioned size is slightly bigger than the requested capacity. Indeed, the CSI for PowerMax reserves some space for the meta data of the filesystem.

Quota per namespace

  • Kubernetes allows defining resource quotas to limit the usage of compute and storage resources of the cluster. The quotas are given per namespace. The storage resource quotas can limit the total amount of storage to be used and the number of PersistentVolumeClaim per namespace.

    It is also possible to scope the quota to a particular storage class like in the example below:

    cat <<EOF > storage-resources.yaml

    apiVersion: v1

    kind: ResourceQuota

    metadata:

      name: storage-resources

    spec:

      hard:

        powermax.storageclass.storage.k8s.io/requests.storage: "500Gi"

        powermax.storageclass.storage.k8s.io/persistentvolumeclaims: 10000

    EOF

    kubectl create -f ./storage-resources.yaml --namespace=test

    Check the quotas definitions for a namespace with:

    kubectl describe quota storage-resources --namespace=test

    Name:                                                        storage-resources

    Namespace:                                                   test

    Resource                                                     Used  Hard

    --------                                                     ----  ----

    powermax.storageclass.storage.k8s.io/persistentvolumeclaims  2     10k

    powermax.storageclass.storage.k8s.io/requests.storage        16Gi  500Gi

Quota per Persistent Volume

  • To paraphrase Kubernetes official documentation, PVs are resources in the cluster. PVCs are requests for those resources and act as claim checks to the resource.

    This means that within the pod definition the PersitentVolumeClaim is just a request, and it will be fulfilled only if there is an available PersistentVolume that satisfies the requirement.

    LimitRange sets at the namespace level it is possible to enforce a minimum and maximum request size. It prevents a pod from bloating all the storage resources and impacts future claims

    cat <<EOF > limit-pvc.yaml

    apiVersion: v1

    kind: LimitRange

    metadata: 

        name: storagelimits

    spec:

        limits:

        - type: PersistentVolumeClaim

          max:

            storage: 100Gi

          min:

            storage: 8Gi

    EOF

    kubectl create -f ./limit-pvc.yaml --namespace=test

    Note: Certain Kubernetes distributions like Rancher allow to set LimitRange by default for any new namespace.

Quota per storage class

  • One effortless way to manage and isolate storage consumption within the cluster is to create different storage pools in the array and map these pools to different storage classes.

    Indeed, every Dell CSI has the option to select the pool to be associated with a different storage class.

    cat <<EOF > storage-class-my-other-pool.yaml

    apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1

    kind: StorageClass

    metadata:

        name: powermax-my-other-pool

    provisioner: csi-powermax

    reclaimPolicy: Delete

    parameters:

        SRP: my-other-pool

        SYMID: "000000000001"

    EOF

    kubectl create -f ./storage-class-my-other-pool.yaml

    The CSI driver itself doesn’t give visibility into subscription rates and utilization rates. Therefore, it is important for the PowerMax storage administrator to have proper monitoring in place for the Storage Pool. A good practice to track these metrics is to install the CSM Observability module.

    Note: The quota per StorageClass is less popular with CSI PowerMax as it is a good practice to keep a single storage resource pool for the entire array.

Quotas

  • With shared infrastructure like a Kubernetes cluster, quotas are a useful way to make sure workloads have the appropriate extent of shared resources. Kubernetes offers several mechanisms to limit storage usage.

    These mechanisms are defined and enforced at different layers of the infrastructure (Pod, definition, storage class, namespace).

    If you need an extra-layer of control to protect the credentials, add RBAC support for storage resources on the array side or implement fine-grained quotas for multiple Kubernetes clusters you can add CSM Authorization module.

Home > Workload Solutions > Kubernetes > Canonical Kubernetes > Guides > PowerMax for Kubernetes: Architecture, CSI Integration, and Best Practices > Replication patterns

Replication patterns

  • There are two main strategies to implement a disaster recovery or high availability for Stateful App you can rely of the application to synchronize the data or use volume level replication.

    Certain applications like Elasticsearch, Cassandra and Couchbase replicates their data natively between an odd number of nodes ; while transactional databases like PostgreSQL or MySQL often use a primary/stand-by approach.

    With volume level replication, the storage backend manages the replication of the data between different sites, in the case of PowerMax this is done via Symmetrix Remote Data Facility (SRDF). The application can then access their data from either of the replicated sites.

    CSI/CSM for PowerMax supports three replication types: asynchronous, synchronous, or active-active replication with SRDF metro.  Geographical and availability requirements will dictate which replication mode is best suited to the needs of the application being replicated.

Storage Class

Dell.com Contact Us
Share
United States/English

Home > Workload Solutions > Kubernetes > Canonical Kubernetes > Guides > PowerMax for Kubernetes: Architecture, CSI Integration, and Best Practices > Storage Class

Storage Class

  • A StorageClass defines the infrastructure's type of storage to the users. Each class has distinct characteristics which we can associate with different service levels and data services provided by the storage platform.

    The CSI Driver for PowerMax source code repository gives multiple examples of StorageClass definitions. 0 shows a sample PowerMax StorageClass with only the mandatory options needed to create a LUN in PowerMax and mount the volume using xfs.

    apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1

    kind: StorageClass

    metadata:

      name: powermax

    parameters:

      SRP: SRP_1

      SYMID: "000000000000"

    provisioner: csi-powermax.dellemc.com

    reclaimPolicy: Delete

    volumeBindingMode: Immediate

    Figure 1.   Basic PowerMax Storage Class Definition

    The key attributes that can be modified to be tuned are :

    • parameters : sets the driver parameters (12 Digit serial number of PowerMax array to connect to & attached storage pool)
    • provisioner : sets the value to determine what provisioner will be used. In case of CSI PowerMax that value can be configured in case you want to instantiate multiple drivers on the same cluster albeit a rare use-case.
    • reclaimPolicy : configures whether the volumes will be retained or deleted when the assigned pod is destroyed.
    • volumeBindingMode : controls when a volume will be provisioned. Immediate is the default value and means that the provisioning occurs as soon as the PersistentVolumeClaim is created. Other possible values are discussed in the next example.

    Note: All the StorageClass fields except annotations are immutable. This means that once a StorageClass is configured it is not possible to modify it. Only delete/create allow to change the settings of a named StorageClass.

    Changing a StorageClass parameter(s) may be needed by future versions of the driver, nonetheless, generally speaking, changing the parameters should be done with caution as it can impact already provisioned volumes.

    Figure 2 shows a more exhaustive example of StorageClass for PowerMax. This example covers more options and concepts:

    apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1

    kind: StorageClass

    metadata:

      name: powermax-metro

      annotations:

        storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: true

    parameters:

      SRP: SRP_1

      SYMID: "000000000001"

      ServiceLevel: Diamond

      csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype: xfs

      replication.storage.dell.com/Bias: "true"

      replication.storage.dell.com/RdfGroup: "17"

      replication.storage.dell.com/RdfMode: METRO

      replication.storage.dell.com/RemoteRDFGroup: "19"

      replication.storage.dell.com/RemoteSRP: SRP_1

      replication.storage.dell.com/RemoteSYMID: "000000000002"

      replication.storage.dell.com/RemoteServiceLevel: Diamond

      replication.storage.dell.com/isReplicationEnabled: "true"

    provisioner: csi-powermax.dellemc.com

    reclaimPolicy: Delete

    allowVolumeExpansion: true

    volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

    allowedTopologies:

      - matchLabelExpressions:

          - key: csi-powermax.dellemc.com/000000000001

            values:

              - csi-powermax.dellemc.com

          - key: csi-powermax.dellemc.com/000000000001.fc

            values:

              - csi-powermax.dellemc.com

          - key: csi-powermax.dellemc.com/000000000002

            values:

              - csi-powermax.dellemc.com

          - key: csi-powermax.dellemc.com/000000000002.fc

            values:

              - csi-powermax.dellemc.com

    Figure 2.   PowerMax StorageClass with Optional values

    The new fields presented here are :

    • The annotation named storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class to change the default StorageClass. This means that any PVC without StorageClass defined will use the default. Note only a single StorageClass can possess this attribute, setting up multiple times will prevent Kubernetes from being able to determine a default and volumes will not be provisioned if a StorageClass is not defined for the PVC.
    • parameters : the CSI Driver offers plenty of optional parameters to configure how a volume will be provisioned (e.g. with replication, on which service level, etc.). The samples & official documentation for the driver describe all the possible parameters in more detail.
    • allowVolumeExpansion : to allow or not to expand an existing volume. In the case of PowerMax the expansion can be done “hot” even with a running container & already mounted volume.
    • volumeBindingMode : the value WaitForFirstConsumer means the volume will be provisioned only the Pod is associated to a node according to the scheduling constraint. That option is required when you want to benefit from the Storage Topology feature (cf. allowedTopologies field).
    • allowedTopologies : some Kubernetes infrastructure do not have uniform access to the storage backends. For example, when you have a cluster with nodes that have Fiber Channel connectivity to PowerMax while other nodes do not (e.g. nodes on virtual machine). The matchLabelExpressions help to control what specific access nodes need to be able to schedule Pod and volumes using that StorageClass. More details on the possible expressions and syntax are documented here.

    To access the details of an existing StorageClass (e.g., powermax) just run: kubectl get storageclass powermax -o yaml

    Note: The PowerMax Multiple Availability Zone feature is a closer experience to the Storage Topology as implemented in public cloud. In other words, once enabled, the StorageClass will have almost no parameters and the CSI driver through its settings and connectivity check will connect to right storage array.

Home > Workload Solutions > Kubernetes > Canonical Kubernetes > Guides > PowerMax for Kubernetes: Architecture, CSI Integration, and Best Practices > Unisphere best-practices

Unisphere best-practices

  • All the API calls issued by CSI are against Unisphere for PowerMax therefore it is important to follow a couple of best practices:

    • Use the latest available version of Unisphere: with all releases come API & performance optimizations.
    • Use one Unisphere per PowerMax array: CSI is a heavy API user, having a dedicated Unipshere for PowerMax server per Array ensures the best possible performance of the API.
    • Use an external Unisphere: likewise, to benefit from the best performance and not impact on the internal Unisphere, it is recommended to use an external Unisphere & dedicate the Unisphere to CSI. This allows the embedded Unisphere to be utilized by the storage administrator for other use cases such as feeding data to Dell AIOPs.
    • Use two Unisphere for high-availability: the CSI driver supports to have two Unisphere servers, one main and a backup, this can also help

    Note: In an environment where you have multiple arrays (e.g. 3) if you follow the best practices, you will have 1 Unisphere per array (e.g. 3) and double them for HA (e.g. 6 in the end).

    Workload profile

    Unisphere API & CSI driver optimize by queuing and throttling API requests to avoid impacting active workloads consuming PowerMax storage.

    When certain applications generate large numbers of parallel volume provisioning or deletion requests, it is often preferable to schedule workloads to serialize these operations.

    A concrete example is Migration Toolkit for Virtualization (MTV): in a single run, it can import thousands of VMs, which may trigger an API storm and cause Unisphere API timeouts. In such cases, it is recommended to schedule separate migration jobs for different VM profiles to prevent overload.

    Similarly, for VDI workloads, it is best to warm up environments before business hours to reduce peak-time API pressure.

Volume migration

  • PowerMax CSI driver allows to upgrade an existing volume from non-replicated to replicated and vice-versa.

    That feature named Volume Migration, can be enabled during installation or updated after install.

    The main concept is to tag an existing PowerMax PersistentVolume with the annotation named migration.storage.dell.com/migrate-to and pass the destination StorageClass as a value (e.g. powermax-metro).

    Note: At the time of the publication a migrated PV loses its CSI compliance as it cannot be resize or take snapshot. That feature is considered experimental

Volume Snapshot Class

  • The VolumeSnapshotClass is a similar concept to the StorageClass, it allows the storage administrators to create different classes of service to manage snapshots for the PVCs.

    apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1

    kind: VolumeSnapshotClass

    metadata:

      name: powermax-snapclass

    driver: csi-powermax.dellemc.com

    deletionPolicy: Delete

    parameters:

      SYMID: '000000000001'

    With vanilla CSI for PowerMax the single configurable attribute is the deletionPolicy that allows or not to delete the snapshot on the array in addition to the VolumeSnapshot object in Kubernetes.

    If you use the CSM replication with Metro volumes, you can add the field parameters.SYMID to take a snapshot on both arrays.

    Note: Some distributions like Openshift, Tanzu, Anthos, etc, come with the Custom Resource Definition (CRD) and External Snapshot Controller for snapshot management; Kubernetes vanilla distribution does not.

    The driver documentation gives all the details to deploy the compatible version of the CRD & controller.

Volume Snapshot & Volume Snapshot Content

  • There is a direct analogy with the PersistentVolume resources and a Volume Snapshot in Kubernetes. the VolumeSnapshot is like a PVC, it is a request for a PVC mapped to the Snapshot on the array; while the VolumeSnapshotContent is similar to the PV, which means it maps to the physical snapshot on the array side.

    Below is an example of a request for snapshot creation:

    apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1

    kind: VolumeSnapshot

    metadata:

      name: pvol0-snap1

    spec:

      volumeSnapshotClassName: powermax-snapclass

      source:

        persistentVolumeClaimName: pvol0

    Figure 5 shows a created snapshot output from kubectl get volumesnapshot        

    Name:         snapcontent-3646c777-4c45-4d33-8848-c376fc4f6542

    Namespace:

    Figure 5.   Viewing a snapshot using kubectl describe volumesnapshotcontents.snapshot.storage.k8s.io & Unisphere

    In Unisphere for PowerMax, the storage group view is the best place to see a volume and its snapshots. Note the prefix of the VolumeSnapshotContent is the suffix of the snapshot name in Unisphere. You can also get the same name from status.snapshotHandle.

    Next is an example of how to create a new PVC from a snapshot:

    apiVersion: v1

    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim

    metadata:

      name: restorepvc

    spec:

      storageClassName: powermax

      dataSource:

        name: pvol0-snap1

        kind: VolumeSnapshot

        apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io

      accessModes:

        - ReadWriteOnce

      resources:

        requests:

          storage: 8Gi

    VolumeSnapshot is a namespaced resource, and therefore it cannot be restored in another namespace. If you need to restore a snapshot in a different namespace you can do so with a tool like PowerProtect Data Manager.

    Note: Kubernetes Snapshots provide a snapshot copy of a volume only and not the memory of the running container. So, when you need to restore your data, you must restore the snapshot to a new PVC and reattach your workload (StatefulSet or else) to the newly created PV and restart the workload.

    Note: When you delete a PV that still has snapshots; the LUN is not removed from the array but renamed with the postfix -DS. After the related snapshots are deleted the CSI driver will delete the LUN permanently.

Why use SAN storage with Kubernetes

  • The CSI Driver for PowerMax and other CSI drivers provide native integration between Kubernetes and backend storage systems.

    All tasks related to provisioning a PersistentVolume and its associated block device are delegated via a PersistentVolumeClaim from the Pod definition.

    By using or reusing SAN storage, organizations can immediately leverage existing investments in hardware and operational processes. It is possible to define a portfolio of StorageClasses with varying service levels (e.g., storage type, replication type, backup strategy).

    SAN enables organic consumption of storage within Kubernetes, similar to how it is used in VMware and other compute platforms. With shared storage solutions like SAN, persistent volumes can be accessed from any node in the infrastructure, enabling workload mobility across the Kubernetes cluster.  In Kubernetes environments volumes are presented to individual hosts and remapped as necessary to facilitate workload mobility.  When a pod moves between nodes, the associated volumes are unmounted from one node and mounted on another.

    SAN and shared storage also offer advanced data protection services, such as LUN-level snapshots, remote replication, and disaster recovery integration with industry-standard tools like VMware Site Recovery Manager. When migrating legacy applications to container-based deployments, these services can be preserved while modernizing the application architecture.

    Even for cloud-native applications using modern data platforms like Elasticsearch, Cassandra, and Couchbase, SAN infrastructure can reduce the compute resources required for replication and take advantage of mature data services offered by platforms like Dell PowerMax. SAN infrastructure offers increasing advantages as data requirements scale, providing efficiency and performance for business-critical workloads.
